questions.title: Categorization: Positive vs. Normative Analysis (Set 1)
questions.prompt_template: Classify each of the following statements into either 'Positive' or 'Normative':

Unemployment in the manufacturing sector fell to 4.1% (Case 1C)
High executive compensation is socially unfair and should be capped (Case 1D)

hints: Recall the structural criteria distinguishing Positive from Normative.
Examine whether the condition describes a direct adjustment or a systemic shift.

questions.title: Multi-Step Quantitative Problem: Macro Supply and Demand Foundations (Problem 1)
questions.prompt_template: Consider a multi-stage quantitative model for Macro Supply and Demand Foundations. Phase 1 gives baseline value $A = {val_a}$ and scale parameter $B = {val_b}$. Phase 2 introduces shock parameter $C = {val_c}$. Step 1: Compute intermediate index $X = (A \times B) / 100$. Step 2: Compute intermediate cost or adjustment factor $Y = X + (C \times 1.25)$. Step 3: Calculate the final net equilibrium metric $Z = Y / (1 + ({val_b} / 100))$. Enter your final answer rounded to exactly two decimal places.

intermediate_steps: Step 1: Intermediate index X = (val_a * val_b) / 100.0
Step 2: Total cost or adjustment factor Y = X + (val_c * 1.25)
Step 3: Final equilibrium metric Z = Y / (1.0 + (val_b / 100.0))

hints: Step 1: Multiply {val_a} by {val_b} and divide by 100 to obtain intermediate value X.
Step 2: Calculate the product of {val_c} and 1.25, then add this to X to determine Y.
Step 3: Divide Y by (1 + {val_b}/100) and round the resulting number to 2 decimal places (e.g., 24.56).

options_template.feedback: Correct! Full multi-step calculation verified with exact 2-decimal point precision.
Incorrect: You omitted Step 3 (dividing by the denominator factor).
Incorrect: You omitted the Phase 2 shock parameter in Step 2.

questions.title: Graphical & Vector Analysis: Macro Supply and Demand Foundations (Model 1)
questions.prompt_template: Refer to the standard geometric coordinate model for Macro Supply and Demand Foundations. The initial equilibrium coordinate is located at point $E_0(Q_0 = {q0}, P_0 = \${p0})$. A policy intervention or exogenous macroeconomic shock causes the relevant behavioral curve to shift parallel outward by $\Delta = {shift_mag}$ units. Graphically, how does this shift alter the geometric area representing net economic surplus / total societal welfare?
hints: Track the coordinate movement from E0 to the new intersection point E1.
Determine whether the polygon of net benefits expands or contracts.

options_template.text: The geometric surplus area expands, shifting equilibrium price and quantity in the direction of the vector shock.
options_template.feedback: Correct! An outward shift of the frontier expands the boundary of welfare and production.

options_template.text: The coordinate remains fixed because non-price determinants only cause movement along existing curves.
options_template.feedback: Incorrect: An exogenous shock shifts the entire curve, relocating the equilibrium coordinate.

options_template.text: Total surplus immediately contracts to zero due to catastrophic allocative failure.
options_template.feedback: Incorrect: Normal shifts adjust prices to re-establish market-clearing equilibrium.

options_template.text: The curve pivots inward along the vertical axis, eliminating consumer reservation price.
options_template.feedback: Incorrect: Parallel shocks maintain identical slopes while translating intercepts.

questions.title: Empirical Policy & Critical Evaluation: Macro Supply and Demand Foundations (Case 1)
questions.prompt_template: Economic analysts are evaluating an empirical policy reform involving Macro Supply and Demand Foundations. Proponents assert that the statutory intervention will maximize public welfare. However, empirical researchers at UC Berkeley and the Federal Reserve caution that secondary behavioral adjustments may induce unintended consequences. Which of the following represents the most rigorous economic evaluation of this scenario?
hints: Remember that economic agents optimize across all available behavioral margins, not just statutory intent.
Consider the Peltzman effect, tax avoidance, or unexpected capital flight.

options_template.text: Statutory intentions are always realized with 100% mechanical fidelity because human agents do not respond to altered price incentives.
options_template.feedback: Incorrect: The fundamental postulate of economics is that individuals alter actions predictably when marginal incentives change.

options_template.text: Agents adjust their behavioral choices at the margin, meaning net welfare depends on the interplay between statutory goals, price elasticity, and deadweight distortions.
options_template.feedback: Correct! Thorough economic evaluation accounts for behavioral elasticity, tax incidence, and welfare trade-offs.

options_template.text: All government policy interventions permanently destroy all consumer surplus regardless of market failure presence.
options_template.feedback: Incorrect: Corrective interventions addressing externalities or public goods can improve allocative efficiency.

options_template.text: Economic models are purely theoretical constructs with zero empirical relevance to municipal or national policy.
options_template.feedback: Incorrect: Modern economics relies heavily on econometric data and causal identification.
